fabrications.carrier_title: Review: Five Underwater Writing Slates Tested on Reef Surveys
fabrications.carrier_doc:
A good underwater slate is one of the cheapest and most important tools a survey diver owns. We tested five popular models over three weeks of reef work, looking at writing surface, size, attachment options and how well they held up to sand and sun.

The A4 clipboard slate with replaceable waterproof paper was the clear favourite for long transects. It held pre-printed data sheets securely and the bungee pencil holder never failed. The smaller wrist slate was handy for quick species notes but too cramped for full survey forms.

{INJECTION}

Two budget slates used a matte plastic surface that worked with ordinary pencils, but they scratched quickly and became hard to read after a week. The roll-up slate packed flat for travel and impressed us more than expected, although it curled in strong surge. Whichever model you choose, attach it with a coiled lanyard rather than a straight cord, and wash it in fresh water after every dive to stop salt crust from building up.

fabrications.carrier_title: Ultra-Low Temperature Freezers: A Buyer's Guide for Research Labs
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Ultra-low temperature freezers keep biological samples at around minus eighty degrees Celsius, and they are among the most energy-hungry devices in any lab. Choosing the right model affects running costs, noise and the long-term integrity of your collection.

Upright freezers are the most common choice because they make inventory easier and take up less floor space. Chest freezers hold temperature slightly better when the lid is opened, but racks are awkward to reach.

{INJECTION}

Modern units with variable-speed compressors and natural refrigerants can use less than half the energy of models sold a decade ago. Check the warm-up time specification, which tells you how long the cabinet stays below minus sixty if power fails. Remote alarms that send messages to a phone are now standard and worth enabling. Plan for regular defrosting, and keep the condenser filter clean, since dust buildup is a leading cause of compressor failure. Finally, budget for a service contract, as repairs on these units can be expensive and slow.

fabrications.carrier_title: Forum thread: Budget underwater housing for a compact camera?
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Original post: I'm a grad student starting reef surveys next season and need a housing for a compact camera. My budget is limited. Is a manufacturer housing worth the extra money, or are third-party housings fine to forty metres?

Reply 1: I've used a third-party polycarbonate housing for four seasons with no floods. The key is maintenance. Clean and lightly grease the O-ring after every trip, and do a dunk test in a rinse tank before each dive.

{INJECTION}

Reply 2: Manufacturer housings usually have better button feel and a more precise fit, which matters with thick gloves. If you can stretch your budget, get one with a vacuum leak detector. It has saved my camera twice.

Reply 3: Don't forget a wide-angle wet lens. Reef work in murky water benefits from getting close to the subject. Also buy a lanyard so you can let go of the housing during safety stops without losing it.

fabrications.carrier_title: Dive Safety Bulletin: Choosing and Deploying Surface Marker Buoys
fabrications.carrier_doc:
A surface marker buoy, or SMB, tells boat traffic and your support crew where you are. Every diver on a research team should carry one and practice deploying it, yet incidents show that many still struggle when it matters.

There are two main types. Open-ended buoys are simple and cheap, but they can lose air if they tip over at the surface. Closed buoys with an overpressure valve stay upright and are easier to see in chop. A length of at least one metre and a bright orange or yellow colour are recommended.

{INJECTION}

Use a finger spool rather than a large reel for most reef dives, as spools are less likely to jam. Deploy the buoy from a stable position a few metres below your safety stop, keeping the line clear of your gear. Practise the skill in a pool at least twice a year. Finally, write your name and boat name on the buoy in permanent marker, so that a lost buoy can be traced back to its owner.

fabrications.carrier_title: Protocol: Tissue DNA Extraction Kit, Marine Invertebrate Supplement
fabrications.carrier_doc:
This supplement adapts the standard tissue extraction protocol for marine invertebrates, including corals, sponges and soft-bodied cnidarians. These tissues often contain mucus, pigments and calcium carbonate that can inhibit downstream reactions.

Step 1. Remove up to 25 mg of tissue and place it in a 1.5 ml tube. For calcified samples, scrape tissue from the skeleton with a sterile blade before weighing.

Step 2. Add 180 microlitres of lysis buffer and 20 microlitres of proteinase K. Vortex and incubate at 56 degrees Celsius overnight.

{INJECTION}

Step 3. Centrifuge briefly to remove skeletal fragments, then transfer the supernatant to a new tube. Add the supplied inhibitor removal solution and mix by inversion.

Step 4. Load the mixture onto the spin column and follow the wash steps in the main protocol. Elute in 100 microlitres of warm elution buffer. Expected yields range from 2 to 15 micrograms depending on tissue type and preservation method.
